entries.title: Turkey: 162 arrested in LGBTQ+ raids
entries.summary: Turkish authorities have arrested at least 162 people in a weekend crackdown on the country's LGBTQ+ community. Ankara says police raids on gay bars and other venues are aimed at protecting family values.
entries.content:
Turkey

Turkey: 162 arrested in LGBTQ+ raids

September 13, 2026

Turkish authorities have arrested at least 162 people in a weekend crackdown on the country's LGBTQ+ community. Ankara says police raids on gay bars and other venues are aimed at protecting family values.

Turkish police have arrested at least 162 people and searched the offices of six LGBTQ+ associations in weekend raids designed to support the country's campaign to protect family values.

The Ankara-based LGBTQ+ rights group Kaos GL claimed that beyond arrests, the government had also cut access to dozens of websites and social media accounts belonging to associate groups and rights advocates.

Government says its fulfilling duty to 'protect families and children'

Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said investigations — prompted by accusations of prostitution and obscenity — were coordinated by prosecutors in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Aydin and Mersin and involved judicial proceedings against 162 suspects, nine associations and 13 businesses across 15 provinces.

"As per the duty to protect families and children given to the state by the constitution, no criminal organization, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated!" Gurlek added in a social media post.

Authorities say they seized drugs, digital equipment, smuggled alcohol and a gun in weekend police operations targeting gay bars and night clubs as well as a hammam that was said to be a place of prostitution.

The Istanbul prosecutor's office added that it had found evidence indicating that children and minors were being inappropriately swayed on issues tied to sexual orientation and gender identity.

Rights groups say the government is unfairly targeting the LGBTQ+ community, with Kaos GL saying that it had been accused of making "posts containing obscenities" accessible to children.

Erdogan scapegoats LGBTQ+ 'perverts' for falling birthrates, avoiding actual contributing factors

The weekend police operation was dubbed "My Family is Safe" by the government and was part of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's "Decade of Family and Population" scheme, which is designed to reverse plummeting birthrates in the aging country.

Authorities say it was intended to make sure that society does not see LGBTQ+ activity as "normal" and that raids were carried out to "protect children, the institution of the family, and our shared moral values."

Although same-sex relations are not illegal in the country, homophobia is rife, with President Erdogan blaming LGBTQ "perverts" for Turkey's rapidly declining birthrates.

That would seem a rhetorical diversion from the actual complexity of reasons for the decline, which Erdogan — who has ruled as the country's authoritarian president since 2014 as well as serving as its influential prime minister for 10 years before that — has called "a disaster."

Though Turkey's statistical agency, TurkStat, tracked a sharp decline in the total fertility rate between 2013 and 2023 (from 2.11 to 1.51 ), the shift brings birthrates in the country closer to those in other developed nations.

Observers say the real reasons for the drop are more likely of a structural and institutional nature rather than one chalked up to lifestyle.

Turkey's chronically worsening financial crisis, inflation, skyrocketing housing prices, family unfriendly workplace environments, limited access to affordable childcare, and higher educational and employment rates for women are all considered reasons for Turks to postpone having children, as well as for having fewer when they finally do.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

entries.title: Ukraine, Poland say Russia hit Warsaw-bound passenger train
entries.summary: Ukrainian officials accused Russia of a "systemic attack" on its railways following drone strikes near the Polish border, including a hit on a locomotive of a passenger train headed to Warsaw.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine, Poland say Russia hit Warsaw-bound passenger train

September 13, 2026

Ukrainian officials accused Russia of a "systemic attack" on its railways following drone strikes near the Polish border, including a hit on a locomotive of a passenger train headed to Warsaw.

Russia launched two drone strikes on western Ukraine, very near its border with NATO member Poland, Ukrainian and Polish authorities said on Sunday.

One of the drones hit a passenger train locomotive in Volyn, some two kilometers (1.24 miles) from the border crossing.

"The monitoring team gave the train crew advanced warning, and thanks to that, no one was injured," Ukrainian railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia said in online post.

The company later said that a "systemic attack" was happening throughout Ukraine.

Separately, Poland's PKP Intercity confirmed that they have taken control of the affected train following the attack in the Ukrainian territory.

"The train is carrying 206 people. There are no Polish citizens among the passengers," the operator said online. "After completing customs clearance, it will continue its journey towards Warsaw."

Zelenskyy: Locomotive 'deliberately burned'

On Sunday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the locomotive was "deliberately burned"  and a gas station damaged in Volyn.

"It is precisely to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe that Ukrainian men and women fight every day, give their lives, and do not allow the aggression to expand," he said.

Moscow did not immediately comment on the reports.

Ukrainian officials also reported another drone strike on Yahodyn overnight, some half a mile (800 meters) from the Polish border.

The border with Poland serves as essential transit point for military and humanitarian aid.

'Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors' — Ukrainian foreign minister

Commenting on the Yahodyn incident, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the "barbaric" attacks were more than "just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders."

"This is Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners," he said in an English-language post on X.

He urged Ukraine's Western allies to make Russia "feel the consequences of its terror. Not just half-decisions, but uncompromising, powerful steps. Full trade embargo. Full entry bans. Full sanctions on the military-industrial complex."

"Putin needs to understand that his barbarism will be met with decisive action that increases the cost of war for him to an unacceptable level," he added.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

entries.title: Russians on the Goethe-Institut: 'Hostage to politics'
entries.summary: Canceled language exams, disrupted plans to study in Germany, and the disappearance of an important cultural link: DW users shared how the closure of Germany's Goethe-Institut in Russia affects their lives.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Russians on the Goethe-Institut: 'Hostage to politics'

September 13, 2026

Canceled language exams, disrupted plans to study in Germany, and the disappearance of an important cultural link: DW users shared how the closure of Germany's Goethe-Institut in Russia affects their lives.

Germany's Goethe-Institut is set toclose all Russian branches by Sunday, amid one of the worst spats in the history of relations between Russia and Germany.

The Russian Foreign Ministry ordered the closure of the German cultural centers in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and Novosibirsk in response to Berlin's reaction to the attempteddrone attackat Leipzig airport in early August. The German authorities blamed Moscow for organizing the attack and announced sanctions. They include closing the Russian culture and education center in Berlin, known as the Russian House, and the Russian Consulate General in Bonn, as well tightening visa restrictions for Russian citizens. 

"All employees must cease their work in Russia as of September 13, 2026," Goethe-Institut Secretary General Gitte Zschoch said in a statement. "No more books can be borrowed from our libraries, and no further training can be offered. German language teachers are losing an important source of professional training and support. For people in Russia, this further restricts access to the German language, culture and reliable information from and about Germany."

DW asked its users in Russia to share how the closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect them personally. The responses received do not constitute a representative survey. All users shared their stories on conditions of anonymity. Russian authorities labeled DW an "undesirable organization" making every cooperation with the media company a criminal offense.

'We'll have to travel to another country' for German exams

Many DW readers fear that, after the closure of the Goethe-Institut branches, they or their relatives will no longer be able to take exams in Russia for internationally recognized German language certificates.

Some readers pointed out that closing the Goethe-Institut in Russia will hit ethnic Germans willing to relocate back to Germany, or late repatriates, especially hard.

"I no longer live in Russia, having emigrated as a late repatriate, but my parents are still in Russia and were planning to take exams at the Goethe-Institut this fall or winter before submitting their resettlement documents. It looks like they'll have to take the exams in another country, which means additional stress and expenses for them," one reader said.

DW also received responses from parents whose children are learning German and plan to continue their education in Germany.

"My son attends a German school, and now we won't be able to take the exam in Russia. We'll have to travel to another country," one message said.

It remains unclear whether exams, language courses and educational programs will continue in Russia in another format or through partner organizations. Several readers expressed hope that at least some services will remain available online.

Goethe-Institute closures hit teachers hard

The closure of the institute will affect not only those planning to move to Germany or enroll at a German university. A German language teacher from the Moscow region told DW that her school had cooperated with the Goethe-Institut for more than 15 years.

"This partnership was one of the most important pillars of our work. The institute supported us with high-quality teaching materials and provided modern books and publications about life in Germany, helping us make lessons engaging and relevant. Our students attended additional courses, and many successfully passed the Goethe certificate exams," she wrote.

"I teach German and can't find a job in Russia," another teacher told DW.

"It's terrible. I'm a German teacher, and I feel professionally stranded and lost," a third wrote.

Despite the restrictions imposed since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine in 2022, demand for the institute's services remained high. According to the Goethe-Institut, around 10,000 people studied German through its programs and partnerships in 2025. Before 2023, that number used to stand at around 16,000 people. The institute administered roughly 22,000 exams, and its libraries were visited by 6,700 people in 2025.

'Culture has become a hostage to political decisions'

Many readers perceive what is happening as another stage in the destruction of ties between Russia and Germany.

"We would like cultural relations between the Russian Federation and Germany not to be destroyed," one DW user responded. "It is sad to realize that culture has become a hostage to political decisions. The closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect people who have no way of influencing politicians."

Some DW readers from Russia specifically draw attention to the responsibility of politicians. One reader called the decision to close the institutes another step toward isolating the country and wondered why its consequences affect ordinary citizens rather than the Russian politicians who make such decisions.

"Why can the people making decisions to isolate Russia from Europe simultaneously provide their own children and close relatives with a European education and a European way of life?" a DW user asked, proposing a ban on the education of the children and close relatives of members of Russia's top leadership at universities in Germany and other EU countries.

Part of the audience considers Moscow's decision expected.

"The closure of the branches looks like a logical response to the closure of the Russian House in Germany. Could it have been otherwise? It is a pity that cultural and humanitarian ties between the countries are becoming hostages to politics," one reader wrote.

Some Russians hold Germany responsible for deteriorating relationship

Some Russians however believe that closing the Goethe-Institut branches in Russia was the right step and blame Germany for the recent escalation of the conflict with Russia.

"German authorities have buried cultural cooperation with Russia by shutting down the Russian House. The responsibility lies entirely with the German side, " said one of the survey participants.

A bilateral intergovernmental agreement between Russia and Germany from 2011 regulates the work of the Russian House in Berlin and the Goethe-Institut's branches in Russia. It obliges both countries, on the basis of reciprocity, to ensure conditions necessary for the operation of their cultural centers. However, it does not in any way provide for the automatic closure of one country's cultural centers in response to the other country doing so.

President of the Goethe-Institut Gesche Joost called the closure of its branches in Russia "the end of an era in German-Russian cultural relations."

According to its website, the Goethe-Institut has 154 branches in 100 countries. This number includes the three branches in Russia that are now being closed.

entries.title: Croatia: 'Monster' fire triggers evacuation on Brac island
entries.summary: A rapidly spreading wildfire threatened homes and tourist accommodations on the Croatian island of Brac, with firefighters battling the blaze overnight.
entries.content:
Croatia

Croatia: 'Monster' fire triggers evacuation on Brac island

September 13, 2026

A rapidly spreading wildfire threatened homes and tourist accommodations on the Croatian island of Brac, with firefighters battling the blaze overnight.

Nearly 700 people were evacuated amid a wildfire on the Adriatic island of Brac, Croatian media outlets reported on Sunday, following a tense night which saw hundreds of firefighters defending homes and tourist accommodations from the approaching blaze.

The situation was especially dramatic near the small town of Milna on the island's western coast.

"Last night was a disaster. It was simply impossible," Milna Mayor Frane Lozic told Net.hr news outlet. "I would have not believed that [the fire] can wipe out everything in its path so quickly."

The fire was first reported on Thursday, but firefighting efforts were complicated by inaccessible terrain.

Even so, Lozic said that the authorities believed they had the situation in hand by Saturday.

"We thought we got it reined in yesterday, that it is all over, and then it happened: Sea wind starts blowing at 9 p.m. and out of nowhere, there is a monster," he said.

No deaths reported in blaze

Tourist ships joined the rescue efforts overnight, with many tourists spending the night at the beach, waiting to be evacuated.

No deaths were reported due to the blaze. However, one 76-year-old Croatian woman was hospitalized in critical condition, according to Index.hr news portal. The woman is believed to have fallen off a ship during the evacuation process. A 27-year-old man required medical aid for smoke inhalation and was then released.

Authorities estimated some 3,500 hectares (8,600 acres) were affected by the fire, according to a report by the AFP news agency.

Officials confirmed some buildings were damaged, but said it was too early for a full damage assessment.

Firefighting planes active on the scene

As of Sunday morning, Croatian authorities said there were no more "open fires" but added teams were still in the field to prevent reignition. Four specialized firefighting planes are also operating in the area.

Two government ministers and the head of Croatia's national firefighting service are set to attend a high-level meeting on Brac this afternoon with local officials and leaders of the local firefighting teams, after which they are expected to provide more information about the blaze.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Vanuatu ferry capsize leaves one dead, 30 missing
entries.summary: Rescue efforts have been slow after a South Pacific inter-island ferry sank in bad weather on Friday. An investigation has already begun into negligence on the part of the operator.
entries.content:
Asia

Vanuatu ferry capsize leaves one dead, 30 missing

September 13, 2026

Rescue efforts have been slow after a South Pacific inter-island ferry sank in bad weather on Friday. An investigation has already begun into negligence on the part of the operator.

At least one person has died and another 30 remain missing after an inter-island ferry in Vanuatu sank in poor weather on Friday.

The South Pacific archipelagic island nation with a population of just under 350,000 is located about 1,750 kilometers (1,090 miles) east of Australia.

The vessel went down in very heavy seas somewhere between the islands of Santo and Ambae, according to authorities.

The MV Matui, operated by the Tui Shipping Agency, set sail Friday from Santo with more than 40 passengers and crew but never arrived in Ambae.

Prime Minister Jotham Napat's office on Sunday morning said that one body had been recovered, 15 passengers had been "accounted for alive" and "over 30 people are missing at sea."

Napat's office took charge of the search and rescue effort on Sunday afternoon after the prime minister expressed frustration over being unable to reach senior officials.

In a statement, Napat's office said, "Search and rescue operations are continuing," adding that the search "in open waters is being eased off whilst efforts ‌move ​toward a search along the southeast coast, where currents may have carried survivors."

"To the survivors, we pray for your strength and recovery. To ⁠the ​families of those missing and those we ​have lost, please know that the nation stands with you in this time of grief," ​the statement continued.

Napat's office also announced that an investigation into the incident had already been launched amid suspicion of negligence on the part of operator Tui.

"This loss appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded," it said, "and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel."

Local frustration at lack of urgency from authorities

Reports of how the rescue effort began are hazy, with Vanuatu parliamentary representative Matai Seremaiah — who took part in the search — telling New Zealand public broadcaster RNZ that a crew member had swam ashore and "alerted us that the ship had capsized."

French news agency AFP cited a hotel owner on Santo who told reporters an employee of his had pulled a survivor in a life vest to shore on Saturday afternoon and authorities were immediately alerted.

It is unclear if these accounts refer to the same survivor.

"He looked like he had been in the bathtub for 25 hours — he was wrinkled up and white. He was cold," said hotel owner Ashley Beveridge.

"There was no rescue started until this guy got washed up on our beach — lucky he got washed up in an inhabited area," he added.

Beveridge told AFP that locals had expressed great frustration at the lack of urgency shown by authorities, with private citizens mobilizing cargo ships and a plane on Saturday afternoon to search for survivors on their own.

The Maritime Rescue Coordination Center (MRCC) in Noumea, New Caledonia, has said it is now assisting in the search effort.

A French Armed Forces aircraft from New Caledonia was also deployed on Sunday morning.

The MRCC said that 12 people had been located Sunday morning.

Local media reported that survivors were being treated at Northern Provincial hospital on Santo Island.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Indonesia rescuers search for 130 people after ferry sinks
entries.summary: The ship was carrying over 240 people in the Java Sea when it ran into bad weather. Officials say six people have died and 130 are still missing.
entries.content:
Indonesia

Indonesia rescuers search for 130 people after ferry sinks

Published September 13, 2026last updated September 13, 2026

The ship was carrying over 240 people in the Java Sea when it ran into bad weather. Officials say six people have died and 130 are still missing.

An Indonesian passenger ship carrying 243 people sank in the Java Sea on Sunday after it was hit by bad weather, local authorities said.

Officials said six people had died, while 107 were brought to safety and some 130 passengers were still missing.

"We have carried out efforts to search for victims to the fullest extent. There were passengers who ... had already been successfully evacuated by the units at the scene," I Putu Sudayana, head of the Banjarmasin Search and Rescue Office, told reporters.

The Virgo Transport 8 was traveling from Indonesia's second-largest city of Surabaya to Banjarmasin, the capital of South Kalimantan province on Borneo island.

It departed on Saturday at 10:13 a.m. local time (0330 UTC), but the ship's operator lost contact with the vessel early Sunday amid bad weather. It was scheduled to arrive in Banjarmasin at about 2 p.m. local time on (0700 UTC) Sunday.

Search operation underway

Search and rescue teams launched an operation after the operator alerted authorities. Ships and a helicopter were deployed to the vessel's last known location.

"The ship's operator reported the incident to authorities after receiving information that the vessel had encountered bad weather," Sudayana said in an earlier video briefing.

The ship's last known position was in the Java Sea, roughly 148 kilometers (92 miles) from a pier in Banjarmasin, according to the Associated Press.

Sudayana added that authorities were mobilizing all available personnel and equipment given the large number of people aboard. The agency was coordinating with maritime authorities while closely monitoring weather conditions in the area, he said.

Indonesia, a nation of roughly 17,000 islands, relies heavily on ferries for transportation, with sea travel often cheaper and more accessible than flying. But safety enforcement across the country's maritime sector has been inconsistent, contributing to a comparatively high rate of accidents.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Germany: Lower Saxony local polls in focus after AfD win
entries.summary: The northwestern state of Lower Saxony is holding local elections that are being seen as a gauge of support for the far-right AfD party. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Lower Saxony local polls in focus after AfD win

Published September 11, 2026last updated September 13, 2026

The northwestern state of Lower Saxony is holding local elections that are being seen as a gauge of support for the far-right AfD party. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Local polls in the state of Lower Saxony are drawing unusual attention after the landslide AfD win in neighboring Saxony-Anhalt
  • A new poll has shown that the far-right party is continuing to gain in popularity nationwide
  • Shipping problems caused by low water levels in the Rhine could take a big economic toll this year, according to experts
  • Former Chancellor Angela Merkel has warned that truth and lies are increasingly being blurred, including by people in power
  • Merkel acknowledged that some decisions during her time as chancellor helped fuel support for the AfD

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of Friday, September 11 through Sunday, September 13:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Lower Saxony local election: Voters face long wait times

Lower Saxony local election: Voters face long wait times

Voter turnout in Lower Saxony has been higher than it was during the 2021 local elections. In some places, voters had to wait to cast their ballots.

According to NDR reporters, wait times in Hanover's Südstadt district were as long as 40 minutes. Long lines formed at polling places in Hanover and other locations.

The polling stations will close at 6 p.m. local time (1600 GMT).

The initial results from the direct mayoral elections are not expected until 7 p.m., while the preliminary statewide district results are not expected until Monday morning.

Skip next section Politicians outraged by apparent antisemitic attack in Berlin

Politicians outraged by apparent antisemitic attack in Berlin

Politicians have reacted with horror to an apparent antisemitic attack in Berlin on the night into Friday.

A group of men verbally abused a woman with antisemitic slurs on Torstrasse in the central district of Mitte before one of them attacked the 43-year-old with a broken bottle, according to police.

The Left Party in Berlin stated that this particular weekend — when Jews celebrate the New Year holiday of Rosh Hashanah — should "be filled with joy, hope, and a sense of new beginnings. Instead, a Jewish woman in Berlin had to defend herself against physical violence."

The party stressed that it was unacceptable and added that wearing a Star of David must "always and everywhere be possible without danger."

Meanwhile, Werner Graf, leader of the Green Party faction in the Berlin House of Representatives, spoke about the "growing antisemitism coming from all political quarters."

Graf said one of the next state government's "central tasks" would be to intensify the fight against antisemitism. Elections for the Berlin House of Representatives and the district councils will be held this coming weekend.

Skip next section Hiker convinced of bear attack at sound of rutting deer

Hiker convinced of bear attack at sound of rutting deer

A hiker in the German Alps was convinced he was about to be attacked by bears on Saturday evening, prompting him to call a police hotline.

On the open line from a trail near Bad Hindelang, in southern Germany's Allgäu region, officers from the Kempten police department listened to the man's desperate pleas for help and quickly realized that it was not a pack of marauding bears making the ruckus — something that would have been highly unusual — but rather, rutting stags doing their "unmistakable" roaring best to attract a partner on a mating season Saturday night.

Police on Sunday said that they had eventually been able to assure the man that he was in no danger, encouraging him to continue along his way while keeping a safe distance from the excited deer.

Skip next section SPD politician calls for price cap on gas

SPD politician calls for price cap on gas

The ongoing uncertainty in the Middle East caused gas prices in Germany to rise even higher over the weekend.

According to data from the fuel price portal Tankerkönig, the average price of E10 premium gasoline was €2.27 ($2.64) per liter nationwide on Saturday.

The data also showed that drivers paid an average of just under €2.40 for diesel.

These prices are in line with the record highs of E10 premium gasoline from March 2022 and just below the record high of diesel from April of this year.

Brandenburg state premier Dietmar Woidke believes that high gas prices must be capped quickly.

“We urgently need a cap on gas prices,” the Social Democratic Party (SPD) politician told the dpa news agency.

"It's unacceptable for oil companies to rake in windfall profits while millions of commuters struggle with fuel prices that are far too high," he added.

From early May through late June, a fuel rebate of 16.7 cents per liter was in effect in Germany.

According to an estimate by the Ministry of Finance, this cost the federal government approximately €1.6 billion. However, the federal government has rejected a renewal of the program.

Skip next section Turnout in Lower Saxony higher than in the last election

Turnout in Lower Saxony higher than in the last election

The voter turnout in the local election in Lower Saxony appears to be slightly higher than in the previous election.

According to the tally released by the State Election Commission at 12:30 p.m., the turnout was 24.60%.

This figure is 3.31 percentage points higher than the turnout in the last local election five years ago. At that time, voter turnout was 21.29%.

Skip next section More protests planned against AfD and far right

More protests planned against AfD and far right

Demonstrators plan to take to the streets in Dresden and Kiel on Sunday as part of a weekend of protests against the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and populist ideologies.

The rallies have largely been prompted by the recent landslide win by the AfD in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the party has been classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by the state domestic intelligence agency.

In Dresden, the capital of the eastern state of Saxony, where support for the AfD is also strong, a demonstration is planned in the square in front of the city's iconic Semperoper under the motto "Time for action."

In Kiel, situated on the Baltic Sea, unions, environmental associations and other groups have called for a protest with the slogan "Not again is now!" in reference to the wish to avoid a repeat of Germany's Nazi period.

Organizers say they want to show "solidarity with all those affected in Saxony-Anhalt" and send a clear signal of opposition to the AfD and its far-right ideology, which many see as anti-democratic.

On Saturday, there were particularly large demonstrations in Düsseldorf, Hamburg, Berlin and Munich, with other smaller rallies taking place in Magdeburg — the capital of Saxony-Anhalt — Leipzig, Mainz and Saarbrücken, along with other places.

In Hamburg, some 25,000 people took part and in Düsseldorf around 20,000, according to police estimates.

Skip next section Asylum approval rates climb as applications sink

Asylum approval rates climb as applications sink

The number of new asylum applications in Germany has fallen sharply but the rate of approvals has risen again, according to the latest official figures from the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees (BAMF).

Altogether 39,646 people put in first-time applications for asylum in Germany in the first half of 2026, a steep drop from the 72,818 applications filed in the same period last year.

However, 47.4% of the applications in the first half of this year were approved, as compared with 37.5% of applications in 2025 as a whole.

Families applying for asylum had particular success, accounting for 45.6% of the positive decisions.

The approval rate for people from Afghanistan — the main country of origin for asylum applicants in the first of the year — was 89.3%, with protection granted to Afghan women in nearly 95% of cases.

This can be attributed to a European Court of Justice decision in 2024 that women from Afghanistan are generally entitled to protection because they are at risk of gender-based persecution under the Taliban regime.

Skip next section Low Rhine water levels expected to cause 'immense' economic damage

Low Rhine water levels expected to cause 'immense' economic damage

The continuing low water levels on the Rhine — a key transport waterway for Germany — are likely to cause grave damage to the country's economy this year, according to the Chamber of Commerce and Industry (IHK) in the western state of Rhineland-Palatinate.

"It is a truly critical situation," spokeswoman Nicole Rabold said.

"Whether the damage will exceed that of 2018 remains to be seen," she said, but added that the economic harm was already expected to be "immense."

2018 saw a previous record low of 25 centimeters (9.8 inches) measured at the key water gauge at Kaub, a major transport chokepoint.

The level at the Kaub gauge, which indicates the viability of freight shipping to operators, is currently still below 25 cm, while earlier this year, it even fell into single digits.

The river becomes nearly unusable for freight transport at a gauge level of 35 cm, though operators are free to take their own decisions on whether to continue with shipping.

The low water levels have been caused by a lack of rainfall and have led to a virtual collapse of freight shipping on the waterway, driving up costs for the industries that rely on waterborne supplies of raw materials.

Skip next section Far-right AfD increases lead over conservatives — poll

Far-right AfD increases lead over conservatives — poll

A new nationwide opinion poll released on Sunday has shown further gains for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party following its major win in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt last week.

The populist opposition party climbed one percentage point to reach 29%, with the conservative bloc of Chancellor Friedrich Merz — made up of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU) — remaining unchanged at 20%.

The opposition Green Party was the only other major party to improve its popularity rating, gaining one point to reach 14% and overtake junior coalition party the Social Democrats (SPD) on 13%.

The Left party was also unchanged at 10%.

The next federal election is scheduled for 2029. The survey was carried out by the polling institute Insa and commissioned by the Bild tabloid.

Skip next section Lower Saxony local polls under scrutiny after far-right win

Lower Saxony local polls under scrutiny after far-right win

Residents in the northwestern state of Lower Saxony are voting for  mayors, district administrators and local councils in elections that are drawing unusual attention after the far-right Alternative for Germany's (AfD's) huge win in Saxony-Anhalt last week. 

The local polls come ahead of key state elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern on September 20 that will also be closely watched as the AfD gains popularity across the country.

However, the party still has much less support in western states than in those in what used to be communist East Germany, with the AfD achieving just 4.6% at district level in the 2021 local elections in Lower Saxony.

Some 6.3 million people are eligible to vote in Sunday's elections.

The massive job cuts taking place at car manufacturer Volkswagen are likely to loom large in voters' minds, as Lower Saxony is home to Volkswagen's HQ and six of its ‌plants, as well as being a key shareholder in the company.

Any run-off elections will take place across the state on September 27.

Skip next section Welcome back to our coverage

Welcome back to our coverage

We are resuming our coverage of all things German on Sunday as local elections get underway in the northwestern state of Lower Saxony.

They are drawing unusual attention in light of last week's landslide victory for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

With two key state elections still to come this year, results for the AfD, which continues to gain support across the country, will be closely monitored.

This comes as the Chamber of Industry and Commerce in the state of Rhineland-Palatinate warns of a "really critical situation" for industry as low water levels in the Rhine continue to hinder shipping.

Read on for more stories from and about Germany on September 13.

Thank you for joining us today.

We will be back with more later on Sunday. Bis bald!

WATCH: Is Germany's love of the Wild West politically correct?

For many decades, romanticized tales of the US Wild West have been popular in Germany. But these stories can be difficult for Native Americans to accept.

Skip next section CSU leader Söder rules out internal move to oust under-fire Merz

CSU leader Söder rules out internal move to oust under-fire Merz

Markus Söder, leader of the Christian Democratic Union's (CDU) Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union, or CSU, has ruled out an internal move to oust the under-pressure chancellor, Friedrich Merz.

Merz has faced growing criticism in recent months for the sluggish pace of promised reforms and amid a surge by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which won the most votes in a state election in Saxony-Anhalt last week.

Asked by the Bild newspaper if there were plans to remove Merz, Söder said, "certainly not from the CSU."

"I am not responsible for the CDU; I am not its chairman. But I can say that for the CSU," Söder added.

Söder said he still believes Merz is the right man to lead the government and push through reforms, urging the center-right alliance to "not let the AfD drive a wedge between us now."

Skip next section France defeats host Germany to reach women's basketball World Cup final

France defeats host Germany to reach women's basketball World Cup final

France beat Germany, the hosts, 86–64 on Saturday to qualify for the women's basketball World Cup final.

Among the 12,650 fans in the German capital were German men's basketball icons Dirk Nowitzki and Dennis Schröder, but they could not cheer their team to victory against the strong French lineup.

Gabby Williams shone for the victors with 22 points, helping France reach the final for the first time.

The United States, the favorites, will take on Spain in the second semifinal later.

The final will take place on Sunday.

entries.title: A Romani artist in Hungary reclaims his identity
entries.summary: Norbert Olah is an artist. He's also Romani. For a long time, he avoided making his ethnic background a theme of his art for fear of being pigeonholed. Then it became his focus.
entries.content:
Hungary

A Romani artist in Hungary reclaims his identity

September 13, 2026

Norbert Olah is an artist. He's also Romani. For a long time, he avoided making his ethnic background a theme of his art for fear of being pigeonholed. Then it became his focus.

The painting on the canvas is of a man playing chess with a robot. The color on his face is still damp and glistening. Norbert Olah was working into the early hours: The Bura Galeria in Budapest has been his studio all summer. He finds it easiest to concentrate at night, when the Hungarian capital gradually falls silent.

Olah has taped foil and cardboard over the tiled floor at the back of the gallery. Pots of brushes, tubes of paint, pencil sketches, and, over and over again, pictures that include the blue-and-green Roma flag line the room.

Norbert Olah is an artist. He's also Romani. For a long time, he deliberately left this part of his identity out of his art. Not because his ethnicity wasn't important to him, but because he didn't want to be labeled a "Romani artist."

"There are so many prejudices about Roma culture and Roma art," Olah says. "The art scene regards it as naïve, unprofessional, unsophisticated, and kitsch."

But the older Olah got, the harder he found it to ignore his own story in his art. Especially in a country in which being Romani is not just an ethnicity but a political reality.

Life under Orban

The first time Viktor Orban's Fidesz party won an absolute majority in the Hungarian parliamentary elections of 2010, Olah had just finished school and was starting his art course at the Hungarian University of Fine Arts in Budapest. At a time of life when the world ought to be opening up, Olah felt more and more barriers were being erected.

Olah was directly affected by Hungary's political reorientation, as both an artist and a Romani. Politics co-opted the cultural scene and made it toe the party line. Roma became the target of hateful rhetoric, including from the prime minister himself. Orban repeatedly called attention to himself with racist comments about Roma.

For the 16 years Orban was in power, Hungary's Roma population, estimated to be around 700,000 people, was caught between official promises of integration and persistent marginalization. Orban's government introduced a state employment program that hired predominantly Romani workers. But instead of helping them gain a foothold in the job market, many Romani found themselves trapped in insecure, poorly paid, temporary jobs. The government did little to implement real change. Romani in Hungary are still disproportionately affected by poverty and social exclusion.

There came a point when Norbert Olah felt he could no longer stand by and do nothing.

Other people's prejudices

In 2021, during Hungary's biggest independent contemporary art event, the OFF-Biennale Budapest, Olah and his father laid a brick wall directly in front of the entrance to the building that had housed the Roma Parliament, a Roma cultural center with an art collection, archive, library, and events program. The Orban government evicted it in 2016, saying the building was structurally dangerous and promising to repurpose it as a national Roma center. It has stood empty ever since.

The title of Olah's work was "The Romani Artist's Fears." Words like "integration," "assimilation," and "segregation" were chiseled into the bricks. A few weeks later, Olah staged a performance in which he took a sledgehammer to his artwork and smashed it till it collapsed.

In an accompanying text, Olah wrote publicly for the first time about the fears, prejudices, and expectations he encounters as an artist with Roma roots. The text is full of questions. Should a Romani artist's work focus on topics relevant to Roma? What is the relationship between ethnicity and aesthetics? Would people only contact an artist with Roma roots if they were specifically looking for a Romani artist, or would they do so if they needed a Hungarian artist, too?

"Of course we're always looking for answers. But sometimes it's more interesting to look at the question itself," says Olah, picking a piece of crepe masking tape off the floor. "If it feels uncomfortable, it's a good question."

And so Olah has created a new label for Romani artists. The Bura Galeria, established by Romani activists in 2021 in Budapest's District 8, has become the place for it: A platform for contemporary Roma art.

"We're not asking to be accepted by the art scene," said Olah. "We're opening the door and inviting others in."

Open antiziganism

Identity and exclusion, power and the misuse of power — these became central themes for Olah's artistic work. He had no lack of inspiration during the Orban years.

Although Fidesz's policies were hardly favorable to Roma, Orban's party could, for a long time, count on Roma votes — for example, because local employment programs enabled local politicians to pressure socially underprivileged voters. There were also many documented cases of vote-buying. Fidesz was so confident that the majority of Roma would continue to vote for it that it openly fueled the antiziganism still widespread in Hungarian society.

Shortly before the election in April 2026, Fidesz's Janos Lazar, who was minister for transport at the time, spoke out against labor migration with the argument that Hungary still had "domestic reserves," like the Roma, who could "clean the crap out of overflowing toilets" on Intercity trains. The scene appears in Olah's art: A fake election poster depicts a man in a balaclava sitting on a golden toilet, brandishing a toilet brush, with the slogan underneath: "Gypsy Criminals for President."

Opportunity for real change?

Gypsy Criminals is also the name of the artists' collective Olah founded in 2024, along with a friend of his and his miniature pinscher. The term comes from Hungarian crime statistics, and has been used since the 2000s by right-wing politicians to imply that all Roma are criminals. The name is ironic, like many aspects of Olah's work.

Analyses by the foundation Roma for Democracy show that many Roma did not vote for Orban's Fidesz party in the April 2026 parliamentary election. Orban's successor, Peter Magyar, adopted a different tone in relation to Roma as part of his election campaign. He met with members of the Roma minority, and his election manifesto contained a specific paragraph about equal opportunities for Roma. Four of the Tisza party's nine new members of parliament are Romani. One was even elected a deputy speaker of parliament.

Since the election, there has been cautious optimism that the precarious situation of many Roma in Hungary could finally change. On the other hand, nothing has fundamentally changed in the four months since the election, apart from the tone when talking about the ethnic minority. "What I'm seeing right now are mostly symbolic gestures," says Olah.

Roma on Mars

Some of his friends in the more liberal art scene are growing impatient. They would like to see Magyar take a much more liberal course, but Olah is a realist.

"He's a conservative politician," he says. "We elected him to put an end to the Orban system. He didn't promise any more than that." But the election in April was an opportunity for a fresh political start, he adds. "I think in the long run we will live in a normal society again, led by a normal government, that will do some things well and others not so well. As an artist, it will be my job to criticize that."

Olah's work also considers the future. The first pictures for his next project are already up on the wall in his studio. It's Roma futurism: A Romani couple strolling on Mars; a blue-and-green Roma flag on the moon; a weightless astronaut with a traditional Cegled water jug, used by Romani musicians as a percussion instrument. Olah is also planning a two-meter-high space station in the shape of a cartwheel, a symbol of the Romani people.

For Olah, space travel is also a metaphor for social advancement — the desire of people and communities to overcome the barriers they face as a result of their origins, or poverty, or life in a minority. Again, he is asking questions. What if a society were fundamentally recreated from the beginning? If aliens encountered Roma, would they do so without prejudice? What remains of an identity if everything about it changes?

Olah shreds the masking tape between his fingers. More unanswered questions. But that's exactly what makes them so interesting.

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Sweden election: Far right eyes power for 1st time
entries.summary: The populist Sweden Democrats could enter government for the first time if incumbent Ulf Kristersson's bloc wins. The left-wing opposition led by former PM Andersson has seen its lead narrow as election day has neared.
entries.content:
Sweden

Sweden election: Far right eyes power for 1st time

Published September 13, 2026last updated September 13, 2026

The populist Sweden Democrats could enter government for the first time if incumbent Ulf Kristersson's bloc wins. The left-wing opposition led by former PM Andersson has seen its lead narrow as election day has neared.

Sweden is holding a general election on Sunday that will either result in the center-left opposition returning to power after four years or see the far right enter government for the first time.

Opinion polls in the run-up to the election have been predicting an easy win for the left-wing alliance over the right-wing group led by incumbent Ulf Kristersson, which includes the far-right party Sweden Democrats.

But the four-party opposition alliance, led by former Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson, the head of the center-left Social Democrats, has seen that lead narrow as election day has neared.

"We all knew it was going to be a very close election; I've said that all along," Andersson, the first woman to serve as Swedish Prime Minister in 2021-2022, told a rally in the Swedish capital Saturday.

"Now it's up to voters: do they want a government that will be totally dominated by the Sweden Democrats, or do they want a government led by me?"

What do we know about the main parties in Sweden's election?

The Social Democrats have governed in Sweden for most of the last century and remain the country's largest party.

The left-wing bloc has promised to boost the welfare state and address rising costs.

Kristersson's campaign has focused on his government's record of reducing violent and organized crime and clamping down on immigration.

A victory at the ballot box on Sunday would suggest voters approve of that approach, supporters of the right-wing bloc say. Critics have denounced the agenda as undermining civil liberties and unfairly targeting immigrants.

"We can unify parties, voters and issues into joint action. That's why ​we get things ‌done," Kristersson said this week in parliament.

Far right could enter government for first time

Unlike in Germany, where most parties have ruled out working with the far-right Alternative for Germany as part of the political "firewall", Kristersson has promised the Sweden Democrats key government posts if his alliance wins.

The leader of the far-right party, Jimmie Akesson, told a campaign rally in Stockholm on Saturday that the Sweden Democrats "have already won," as the party eyes power for the first time since entering parliament in 2010.

"Sweden is becoming safer, better, and more Swedish," the 47-year-old said.

Akesson is expected to be given the role of migration minister if the right-wing alliance wins on Sunday.

Eight million people are eligible to vote in a country of 10.6 million people. Turnout regularly exceeds 80% in Sweden.

Polling stations close at 8 p.m. (1900 UTC). The first results will be expected several hours later on Sunday night.

Around half of the votes have already been cast in advance.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: France: Attack ruled out in train derailment
entries.summary: More than 40 were injured when a train derailed between Rouen and Caen in Normandy, northwest France, on Friday evening. Investigators say there is "no indication" the incident was deliberate.
entries.content:
France

France: Attack ruled out in train derailment

September 13, 2026

More than 40 were injured when a train derailed between Rouen and Caen in Normandy, northwest France, on Friday evening. Investigators say there is "no indication" the incident was deliberate.

A train derailed on Friday evening between the cities of Rouen and Caen in Normandy, northwest France, authorities said.

The public prosecutor of Rouen, Sebastian Gallois, said Saturday evening that there was "no indication of a malicious act carried out with the deliberate intention of derailing the train, and certainly not of an attack," according to reports in the French media.

Gallois' remarks came after some politicians had suggested earlier on Saturday that the incident might have been the result of sabotage or other criminal activity.

At least 44 people were injured in the accident, which occurred near the municipalities of Cleon and Tourville-la-Riviere at around 7:30 p.m. local time (18:30 UTC), the Seine-Maritime prefect said in a statement.

One of ​the injured, a young woman, was in a critical state and was evacuated by helicopter to Rouen, the local authority added. Her condition has reportedly improved in the hours since.

The train was carrying around 180 passengers when it derailed, national rail company SNCF and the prefect said.

What else do we know about the train derailment?

French Transport Minister Tabarot said 140 firefighters were at the scene.

Local authorities had urged the public to avoid the area.

The French rail network operator SNCF Reseau said traffic on the line had been suspended.

"The priority is to care for the passengers and then to restore safe operating conditions," SNCF Reseau said.

​A police spokesperson had said the train derailed after hitting an unidentified object.

A piece of rail that might have been involved has been found on the track, according to police reports.
